strengths: Novel and clearly motivated threat model: EEB is the first systematic study of backdoor attacks designed to survive subsequent concept erasure in text-to-image diffusion models, filling a genuine gap between the backdoor literature and the unlearning/erasure literature.

Comprehensive experimental scope: the paper evaluates four attack variants (data poisoning, text-encoder, cross-attention, and the new score-based EEBdeep) against six erasure methods including three adversarially robust ones (RECE, RECELER, ADVUNLEARN), across three tasks (celebrity, object, explicit content) and three architectures (SD v1.4, SD v2.1, FLUX/DiT).

Strong empirical rigor and analysis depth: trajectory analysis over erasure checkpoints (Supp. C), ablations of EEBdeep's components (quality/retention losses, templates, alpha sensitivity), trigger selection and multi-trigger studies, and a detectability analysis using WeightWatcher and T2IShield. The finding that EEBdeep persists across ALL tested erasure methods, including adversarially robust ones, is well supported (e.g., 79.72% ASR against RECE on celebrity erasure, up to 16x amplification of explicit content).
Reasonable treatment of ethics: explicit content is censored, an impact statement is provided, experiments use public datasets, and a responsible disclosure plan for code/checkpoints is described.

Reproducibility effort: extensive implementation details (hyperparameters, official codebases used and modifications, 80 prompt templates, compute budgets, runtimes) and a promised minimal code base for reviewers.

The paper is well written with a clear threat model formulation (Section 3.1) distinguishing black-box and graded white-box access, and it honestly discusses limitations such as RECELER's own utility degradation and ESD-X's intrinsic weaknesses in the multi-trigger analysis.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty of the core attack: EEBdata, EEBsurface (Rickrolling), and EEBshallow (EvilEdit) are adapted from prior work, and EEBdeep is essentially a standard self-distillation objective with a trigger loss; the primary novelty is the threat model and evaluation rather than a new attack technique.

The defense analysis is thin. No tested erasure method removes the deep backdoor, and the paper offers only partial detection signals (~90% AUC T2IShield, weight-norm anomalies) rather than an effective mitigation. A defender-oriented contribution (e.g., erasure robust to known poisoning, or certified removal of trigger-target links) would substantially strengthen the work.

Evaluation relies on single third-party classifiers (GCD for celebrities, ResNet-18 for objects, NUDENET for explicit content) without human evaluation or multiple classifiers to validate ASR; main tables lack confidence intervals or significance testing despite ~10-target averaging, and variance is only shown in supplementary figures.

Practical relevance of the strongest result is somewhat constrained: EEBdeep assumes full white-box access and LoRA fine-tuning of a model the attacker then publishes; the paper could more explicitly discuss how defenders on open-source platforms could audit checkpoints before re-release.

Presentation polish issues: leftover internal naming ('DISA attack') appears in Supplement D.3 and F, Eq. 2 contains a formatting error (stray comma), and Table 2 (persistence before erasure) vs. Table 3 (persistence after erasure) results are potentially confusing for readers without clearer signposting.

Some claims are slightly over-stated relative to the evidence, e.g., EEBshallow 'overpowers UCE' on SD v2.1 at 61.32% ASR while its celebrity ASR on SD v1.4 against UCE is 68.88% but near zero against ESD/MACE/RECE, indicating strong method-specific dependence that the abstract-level claims do not convey.

strengths: The paper introduces and clearly formalizes a genuinely new threat model for concept erasure in text-to-image diffusion models (Erasure Evasion Backdoors), which to my knowledge has not been studied before, distinguishing it from prior backdoor attacks on diffusion models and from prompt-based erasure circumvention.

The empirical study is broad and systematic: four attack variants spanning black-box (data poisoning) to white-box access, six erasure methods including three explicitly robust ones (RECE, RECELER, ADVUNLEARN), three erasure tasks (celebrity identity, object, explicit content), and three architectures (SD v1.4, SD v2.1, FLUX), with utility controlled via FID/CLIPScore/retention accuracy.

The proposed EEBdeep attack is a reasonable technical contribution: a self-distillation objective (trigger, retention, and quality losses) that embeds persistent trigger-target links across the whole U-Net, with ablations (Lq, Lr, templates, alpha sensitivity, iteration count) supporting the design choices in the supplementary.

Additional analyses strengthen the contribution: trajectory analysis across erasure iterations, multi-trigger and multi-target injections, trigger selection, detectability discussion (T2IShield AUC, WeightWatcher diagnostics), and a clear responsible-disclosure and impact statement.

The finding that backdoor persistence increases with the depth/breadth of parameter modification, and that erasure methods acting on the same architectural component as the attack are disproportionately vulnerable, yields actionable insight for designing more robust erasure methods.
weaknesses: Threat model plausibility is under-argued. EEB requires the adversary to poison a model or its training data before a well-intentioned third party applies erasure. The paper does not demonstrate a realistic pipeline in which poisoned checkpoints are actually published on platforms like Hugging Face and then sanitized, nor does it discuss whether erasure is typically applied to community checkpoints at scale. The practical relevance therefore rests largely on assumption.

Statistical rigor is limited: the main celebrity results average over ten targets with no confidence intervals or significance testing; several key claims (e.g., the 16x amplification, FLUX results) rely on raw detector counts from a single run, and NUDENET/GCD classifier noise is not characterized. The explicit-content '16x' headline derives from a small base number (e.g., 18 to 38, 52 to 819), and absolute base rates are low, making relative amplification metrics potentially misleading.

Novelty of individual attack components is incremental: EEBsurface and EEBshallow are direct adaptations of RICKROLLING and EVILEDIT, and EEBdeep is a fairly straightforward combination of a distillation-style trigger loss with LoRA fine-tuning. The paper's value is mostly in the new threat framing and evaluation, not in technically novel machinery.

Some results are noisy or internally inconsistent (e.g., EEBdata occasionally reducing post-erasure exposure; large variance in Table 12; ESD-X's high target accuracy acknowledged as confounded), and the paper sometimes interprets these post hoc without deeper analysis.

The defense analysis is preliminary and mostly qualitative: detection is evaluated on a single configuration, WeightWatcher diagnostics only flag the shallow closed-form attack, and no erasure-method modification that mitigates EEB is proposed or tested; the 'diagnostic tool' framing is asserted but not validated by an actual stress-testing protocol.

Key experimental details in the main text (e.g., the '2,000 training iterations for our DISA attack' referencing an attack name that appears nowhere else, leftover notation) suggest rushed writing; a few figures (Figure 3, Figure 6 grid layout) are hard to parse without the supplementary.

Reproducibility is only partially addressed at submission: a minimal code base is promised for reviewers, and full code/checkpoints are deferred until after a responsible-disclosure window, so independent verification is not currently possible.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated threat model: the paper is the first (to the authors' knowledge, plausibly correct) to systematically study backdoors that are designed to survive concept erasure in T2I diffusion models, distinguishing it from prior work on backdoors per se and on prompt-based 'resurrection' of erased concepts.

Comprehensive empirical coverage: four attack variants spanning black-box (EEBdata) to white-box (text encoder, cross-attention, score-level/LoRA), evaluated against six erasure methods including three adversarially robust ones, across three tasks (celebrity, object, explicit content) and three architectures (SD v1.4, SD v2.1, FLUX.1).

EEBdeep is a genuine methodological contribution: a self-distillation trigger loss across the full diffusion pipeline with quality/retention regularization, supported by ablations (Table 8, Table 9 for alpha, Figure 10 for iteration budget) that justify design choices rather than just reporting them.

Honest and useful analysis of failure modes and structure: attack surface alignment (e.g., EEBsurface vs. ADVUNLEARN, EEBshallow vs. UCE), trajectory analysis across erasure checkpoints (Supp. C), the caveat that ESD-X has intrinsically poor erasure, and the RECELER utility-erasure trade-off are all discussed candidly rather than glossed over.

Responsible treatment of a dual-use topic: content censoring, impact statement, staged code/checkpoint release, and a preliminary detectability analysis (T2IShield AUC ~90%, WeightWatcher spectral diagnostics) that gives defenders a starting point.
Good reproducibility posture: full hyperparameters, official codebases of erasure methods, prompt/template lists in Supp. G, and compute accounting in Supp. F.
weaknesses: The headline claims ('up to 82%', 'consistently exposes harmful content') are driven by the best variant (EEBdeep) and best method combinations; against the most robust erasure methods (RECELER) ASR drops to ~19% (celebrity) and ~35% (object), so evasion is not uniformly consistent — the abstract slightly oversells robustness coverage relative to Tables 3-4.

Main results use a single representative trigger (rhWPpSuE) chosen from a small set; while trigger analysis is provided in Supp. E, the generality of conclusions over arbitrary/adversarially optimized triggers remains an assumption.

No error bars, seeds, or variance estimates for the main tables (Tables 3-7), despite ASR estimates over 250 (celebrity) or 100 (object) generations; some gaps between variants (e.g., 74% vs. 82%) may not be statistically robust.

The defense/remedy analysis is largely descriptive: detection via T2IShield and WeightWatcher is demonstrated on one setting (EEBdeep, celebrity), and no attempt is made to actually strengthen an erasure method against EEB (e.g., incorporating trigger-aware terms into adversarial erasure), so the 'diagnostic tool' framing is asserted rather than exercised.

The FLUX study is quite preliminary (two erasure methods, nudity only, and the clean erased FLUX baseline already produces very high unsafe-detection counts, complicating interpretation of relative amplification).

Threat-model practicality for weight-based attacks rests on publishing poisoned open-source checkpoints; the paper does not discuss plausible real-world pathways or the defender's incentive structure in depth, which slightly weakens the significance argument for EEBdeep versus the more realistic EEBdata.

Multiple-trigger experiments (Supp. E) reveal instability (some triggers fail to implant; MACE removes one backdoor but not others) that hints at important dynamics the main narrative does not fully account for.
